tasks.title: Agent-team caps are process-local memory — they stop being controls the moment relay coordinates
tasks.done_when: The spawn concurrency cap and the depth cap are enforced by relay's database rather than by one broker process's memory, demonstrated by two independent claimants racing and exactly one winning
tasks.notes:
Found 2026-07-29 while researching Q8 (one log or two) in docs/agent-orchestration.md.
It is NOT a defect in agent-chat — see the companion task in claude-channels.

## THE FINDING, from source rather than docs

Every safety property agent-chat's agent-teams system has is a SINGLE-NODE-PROCESS
guarantee:

- The spawn concurrency cap is a plain `Set<string>` in the broker process
  (agents/semaphore.ts), default 3 slots. No DB, no lock, no transaction.
- The depth cap (MAX_DEPTH = 2) is checked in `Supervisor.preflight`, synchronously,
  in the same JS call stack as `semaphore.acquire`.
- Name collision is an in-memory `Map` scan (registry.ts `findByName`) — and there
  is a SECOND, independent name check against the log fold
  (`AgentLog.nameIsClaimed`). Two non-transactional sources of truth, not one.
- broker/event-log.ts uses NO transactions at all — no BEGIN/COMMIT, no
  `.transaction()`. Every call is a standalone statement.
- The `events` table has NO unique constraint beyond the PRIMARY KEY. Its only
  indexes are events_target, events_msg_id, events_ref — none UNIQUE.

supervisor.ts states the assumption itself:

  "the semaphore and depth cap need exactly one enforcement point, because
   per-session enforcement is not enforcement"

That is correct, and it stops one step short of what relay needs:
*** PER-PROCESS ENFORCEMENT IS NOT ENFORCEMENT ONCE THERE ARE TWO PROCESSES. ***

## WHY IT IS RELAY'S PROBLEM AND NOT AGENT-CHAT'S

On one machine with one broker, in-memory state is a legitimate and sufficient
enforcement point — arguably the RIGHT one, since it needs no coordination. The
moment relay is the coordinator the premise is void: relay is multi-machine by
design, and two runners on two laptops share no `Set`.

So these are not bugs to report upstream. They are properties that DO NOT PORT,
and the porting side owns them. Filing them only in claude-channels would read as
a bug report for something that is not broken there.

## WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS

MAX_DEPTH and the 3-slot semaphore are the two controls standing between a
compromised or confused requester and a fork bomb. CC-25's §11 audit (2026-07-28)
confirmed both genuinely hold — the 4th spawn is refused, slots are freed rather
than leaked, and depth cannot be lied about because it is read off the parent's
own recorded meta. That audit is sound and this does not contradict it. But it
drove the real classes IN ONE PROCESS, which is exactly the condition that makes
in-memory enforcement work.

If the fold ships without replacing them, relay gains a public HTTPS dispatch path
whose fork-bomb defences silently evaluate to nothing. That is a worse position
than today, where the same controls are real.

## THE FIX PROBABLY ALREADY EXISTS

Q8 produced the pattern and it generalises: a UNIQUE PARTIAL INDEX over a
GENERATED column projecting a value out of `meta`, verified on hosted D1 2026-07-29
(compat-suite.sh, 57/57). "One live run per item" became "one row per attempt".
"At most N live agents per requester" and "depth <= 2" are the same shape of
problem — a constraint over an append-only log rather than a counter in memory.

Depth is the easier of the two: it is already derived from the parent's recorded
row, so it needs a constraint rather than a redesign. Concurrency is harder,
because a cap of N is not a uniqueness property; expect this to need either a
counted projection or an explicit slot-claim row per slot.

## DO NOT

- Do not fold this into Q8. Q8 is answered; this is a separate property.
- Do not treat CC-25 (spawn-rate budget) as covering it. That is a RATE limit and
  is still open upstream; this is about the concurrency and depth caps that CC-25
  explicitly verified as working.

Companion task: claude-channels, "MAX_DEPTH and the spawn semaphore are in-memory".

UPDATE 2026-09-18: re-pointed per plan-relay-agent-chat-contracts.md section 6 ('Re-point R-48 at CC-P2, whose rate and slot policy is per service') at CC-114, the filed service caller class task -- CC-P2 gives relay a per-service rate and slot policy enforced by the broker rather than relay's own process memory, which is this task's underlying ask. Not closed: CC-114 builds the enforcement point, but this task's own done-when (concurrency/depth caps enforced by relay's database, demonstrated by two racing claimants) is not met until relay actually relies on that enforcement instead of its own in-memory caps.

tasks.title: Refuse to dispatch when the running broker is older than agent-chat's dist
tasks.done_when: A relay dispatch against a broker running stale code is refused with a run_refused naming the staleness, rather than silently spawning an agent with old behaviour — demonstrated by rebuilding agent-chat without restarting its broker and watching a dispatch refuse
tasks.notes:
Third instance of one shape in a single day, each a layer deeper:

1. merged is not deployed (relay Worker) — caught by the handoff loop.
2. rebuilt is not installed (agent-chat's dist/cli.js lost its +x when tsc
   rewrote it) — surfaced 30 seconds later as a relay run_refused in another
   project. Fixed by a postbuild chmod.
3. rebuilt is not RUNNING — the broker had been up 2h49m and had loaded
   pre-R-70 code. Caught only because agent-chat prints a warning at spawn.

The third is the dangerous member of the family, because nothing downstream can
see it. R-70 was merged, deployed, rebuilt AND still not in effect; relay
dispatched two agents through that broker while I believed the fix was live.
agent-chat's own warning says why it cannot be repaired after the fact: "a
spawned agent's argv is fixed at spawn time, so it will carry the OLD behaviour
permanently even after a later restart."

agent-chat already computes this — it compares broker load time against dist
mtime and prints the warning on `agent spawn`. relay's executor throws it away:
dispatchToAgentChat reads stdout for the peer name and ignores the rest.

Cheapest fix: have the executor notice that warning on stdout/stderr and refuse
the run with it as the body, so the operator reads "the broker is running stale
code" in agent_digest instead of getting a silently-stale agent. A stronger
version would ask the broker directly, but relay takes no dependency on
agent-chat's internals by policy (dispatch.ts's header names the CLI as the
supported surface), so parsing the warning it already prints is the option that
respects the seam.

R-38 shipped: "how does the MCP surface the schemas to agents?"

## The gap, stated plainly

**Agents never see the registry.** Tool schemas are static Zod enums compiled
into the Worker (`z.enum(ITEM_CONTEXTS)` in mcp-tools.ts / admin-tools.ts).
`type_schemas` appears NOWHERE in the MCP layer — no lookup, no resource, no
describe-schema tool.

So R-33's no-deploy property is **half-real**: an INSERT into `type_schemas`
makes the DATABASE accept a new attribute, but no agent will ever send it,
because the tool schema does not mention it. No deploy is needed for storage;
one is still needed for the agent-facing vocabulary.

## The enabling measurement already exists

Probe 1 (plan doc §2.3, measured on a real phone 2026-07-27): **connectors do
NOT cache the tool set.** A live session picked up `capture_item` without the
connector being re-added. So a registry-driven tool surface would actually
propagate to the phone rather than sitting behind a stale cache. This is the
finding that makes the ticket worth doing rather than theoretical.

## Design direction (not settled — decide in the ticket)

The operator's framing: "ideally autogenerate a tool set per schema."

Recommended shape is a HYBRID, not fully dynamic:

- **Keep the well-known facets as first-class typed parameters.** This is what
  makes voice capture reliable — the model should not need a lookup to say "at
  phone, admin". Losing that would be a real regression on the surface that is
  actually in daily use.
- **Autogenerate per registered kind** for everything else, reading
  `type_schemas` at server construction (`createVoiceServer` / `createAdminServer`
  in index.ts, both currently synchronous — they would need to become async).
- **Expose the registry as an MCP RESOURCE** as well. A resource is precisely
  "here is some data the client can read", which is what a schema registry is,
  and it costs the voice path nothing.

## Constraints and risks

- **Voice latency.** A D1 read on every MCP session init lands on the capture
  path. Measure it; R-38's first signal was ~77ms warm for a whole capture, so
  there is not much headroom before it is noticeable.
- **A bad registry row becomes a broken tool surface.** Today a malformed
  vocabulary is a compile error; after this it is a runtime one, on the door the
  operator uses from a phone. Needs a fallback to the static schema rather than
  failing closed.
- **Test surface.** Tool schemas stop being statically inspectable, so
  mcp-tools.test.ts's assertions about enums have to be rethought.

## Related seam

`worker/src/schema-registry.test.ts` currently asserts the registry seed equals
`ITEM_CONTEXTS`/`ITEM_AREAS`. If tool schemas become registry-driven, that seam
CHANGES rather than disappears — the constants would become the fallback, not
the source of truth, and the test should be rewritten to say so rather than
deleted.

tasks.title: Split `required` into presence + nullable: let an attribute demand an explicit null rather than accepting silent absence
tasks.done_when:
An attribute can be registered as "must be stated explicitly, and null is a
valid statement", and item_create rejects a payload that omits it — while
accepting one that passes it as null. The distinction survives both writer
doors. `required` no longer exists as a single boolean that conflates two
independent axes.
tasks.notes:
Raised by the operator 2026-07-28, from a failure seen on an unrelated project.

## The worry, in their words

Properties being "silently ignored on items that genuinely have a value for it
just because of lack of visibility/awareness in the tooling description or agent
use of the tool". The concern is agent-facing: an agent operates on an item
while blind to part of its state, and nothing anywhere notices.

## `required` today is dead, and would be wrong if implemented naively

`type_schemas.required` (0005:46) is declared, seeded as `0` on all twelve rows,
and referenced by **zero triggers and zero application code**. It enforces
nothing. That is lucky, because the obvious implementation forecloses the case
actually wanted.

A single boolean conflates two **orthogonal** axes:

|  | nullable = yes | nullable = no |
|---|---|---|
| **presence: optional** | today's default — absent means unset | if mentioned, must have a value |
| **presence: required** | **must be stated; `null` is a valid answer** | classic `NOT NULL` |

The top-right cell is the ask. A NOT-NULL-flavoured `required` cannot express
it. So: **two columns, not one boolean.** Migrate `required` out rather than
overloading it — it has no data to preserve, every row is 0.

## The plumbing already exists

`normalizePatch` (`items.ts:298`) keys every field on `!== undefined`, so
*absent* and *explicit null* are already distinct in the write path: absent
leaves the column alone, `null` clears it. Nothing consumes that distinction as
policy. This is a seam to use, not one to build.

## DECIDED: enforcement is create-only

Operator's call, 2026-07-28. `presence=required` is enforced at **item_create**.
`item_update` keeps pure patch semantics — absent still means "do not touch".

Rejected alternatives, recorded so they are not relitigated:

- *Always, full-restate*: every update must restate required attributes, null
  included. Strongest guarantee, but makes every partial edit verbose and would
  push agents toward read-modify-write on a system with no event history.
- *Enforce on read-then-write*: require the fields only if the agent has not
  read the item this session. Targets the real failure most precisely, but needs
  per-session state relay does not have.

The create-only choice means the blind-agent case on EDIT is **not** covered by
this ticket. That is a known, accepted gap — the visibility half is covered
separately, below.

## The visibility half — DONE, 2026-07-28

Found while researching this: `item_update` named its editable fields a **third**
time, by hand, in its Zod `inputSchema`, untied to `META_ATTRS` or
`type_schemas`. Since 0005's comment advertises that adding an attribute is an
INSERT with no deploy, an attribute could become real — triggers accept it,
storage round-trips it, imports populate it — while `item_update` could neither
set it nor mention it. Silent, exactly as described.

`admin-tools.test.ts` now guards it: "registry coverage — no registered
attribute may be invisible". Verified by mutation (added a bogus attr to
`META_ATTRS`, confirmed the test fails, reverted).

## Open questions for the implementation

- Where does create-time enforcement live? The project's stated position is
  "enforcement lives in the DATABASE, not only in the storage module" (0005),
  because a third writer could bypass the storage module. But a BEFORE INSERT
  trigger sees the row, not the *payload* — it cannot distinguish "key absent"
  from "key present and null" once the JSON is assembled. **This may be the
  hardest part of the ticket.** Options: have the doors write a sentinel, or
  accept that presence is an application-layer check while nullability stays a
  trigger one, and document the split honestly.
- Does `item_get` / `item_search` output need to render explicit nulls
  distinctly from absent keys? If the readback cannot show the difference, an
  agent still cannot see it.
- Interaction with R-35 entities, which register in the same table.

tasks.title: Wrangler's user-level OAuth token reaches relay and no ticket closes it — not even account separation
tasks.done_when: A written decision exists on the Wrangler user-OAuth path: either relay administration authenticates through a credential that does not also reach unrelated projects, or the residual is explicitly accepted with the reasoning recorded in docs/r20-token-runbook.md §3. Whichever, docs/logan-corpus-decision.md C4 becomes answerable rather than indefinitely blocked.
tasks.notes:
Filed 2026-07-28. The gap was identified by the R-36 data-handling pass, which
asked the question nobody had: does R-44 actually close this? It does not.

## The gap

~/Library/Preferences/.wrangler/config/default.toml (mode 0600) holds Wrangler's
user-level OAuth `oauth_token` and `refresh_token`. This is how relay itself
deploys, which is why relay needs no API token of its own.

It covers everything the account OWNER can reach. It cannot be scoped at all.
Any process running as the owner can use it — including a headless agent spawned
by the runner (R-3), which is the same path R-13 exists to harden.

## WHY R-44 DOES NOT CLOSE IT — check this before assuming otherwise

R-44's done_when is about credentials belonging to ANOTHER PROJECT:
  "no credential on disk for another project can read relay's D1 or deploy the
   relay Worker"

The Wrangler OAuth pair is not another project's credential. It is the USER's.
After account separation the same human is a member of both accounts, so the
same token still reaches relay. docs/r20-token-runbook.md §3 states this
explicitly and §5 repeats it — the runbook was careful about it, and the
carefulness is why claiming R-44 closes "the credential problem" would be wrong.

R-44 reduces what a PROJECT credential reaches. It does not reduce what an
OWNER credential reaches. Three credentials reach this account; R-20 addressed
one, R-44 addresses the same one more thoroughly, R-45 removes another, and this
ticket is the third.

## Why it is priority 5 and not higher

Unlike the Global API Key (R-45), this credential is LOAD-BEARING — it is the
deploy path. Removing it without a replacement breaks deployment, so this is a
design question rather than a delete. Options sketched by the R-36 pass, none
evaluated:
  - a separate login used only for relay administration
  - staying logged out and authenticating per deploy
  - an account-scoped API token for relay specifically, accepting that D1:Edit
    and Workers Scripts:Edit are still account-wide (so this only helps once
    R-44 has made "the account" mean "relay's account")

That last option shows the sequencing: this ticket gets cheaper AFTER R-44, not
before. Do not attempt it first.

## Consequence if it is never resolved

docs/logan-corpus-decision.md C4 asks for the residual credential reach to be
closed OR explicitly waived in writing. If this path is never addressed, C4 can
only ever be satisfied by waiver — which is legitimate, but should be a decision
someone makes on purpose rather than a condition that quietly never clears.

tasks.title: Headless is a profile default, not an invariant — a runtime surface change can put the brief back in claude's argv
tasks.done_when: Either a dispatched relay agent cannot reach launch-plan.ts's interactive branch by any runtime path, or relay refuses/detects the case rather than assuming it away — and the M8 amendment's headless sentence can state it as enforced rather than defaulted.
tasks.notes:
Found 2026-08-10 by the R-68 review (reviewer r68-argv, partially corroborated by r68-docs). R-68 closed the argv hop on the assumption that relay's agents are headless. Both profiles do declare surface: headless (verified in repo AND in the installed copies at ~/.agent-chat/profiles/), but nothing ENFORCES it at dispatch:

- daemon/src/dispatch.ts validates the profile NAME against the closed set, never the resolved surface.
- agent-chat/src/agents/launch-plan.ts:190 pushes the brief into claude's argv on the non-interactive-else branch: if (input.resume !== true) args.push('--', input.brief).

r68-argv reported a specific chain to reach it — agent_surface rewrites identity.surface (supervisor.ts:861 -> identity.ts:116), teleport then takes identity.surface rather than profile.surface (teleport.ts:300), and the relaunch calls buildLaunchPlan without resume (supervisor.ts:984), so line 190 fires. VERIFICATION STATUS: I confirmed the two endpoints (line 190 exists; dispatch checks the name only). I did NOT walk the middle of that chain — treat it as plausible and unverified rather than established, and verify before building a fix.

Note the reviewer also found plain surfacing alone is clean, because it passes resume: true.

Cheapest partial mitigation if the full chain proves real: have relay assert the resolved surface at dispatch rather than trusting the profile name.

tasks.title: Replace R-70's env denylist with a measured allowlist
tasks.done_when: A dispatched agent's environment is built from a named list of variables rather than the parent environment minus a pattern, demonstrated by spawning an agent that completes real work — including a git push — under it
tasks.notes:
R-70 shipped a denylist (agent-chat src/agents/agent-env.ts), and its own header says plainly that this is the weaker control: it cannot be complete, and a secret in a variable named nothing like a secret still travels.

M8 asks for an allowlist. The reason one was not written is that the set a full Claude Code agent needs is not knowable by reading — relay's own minimalEnv() reached three variables by measurement, twice by watching production fail (env: node: not found, then a Keychain lookup that needed USER). An allowlist that misses a variable breaks every spawn for every agent-chat user.

So this is mostly measurement, not design: spawn real agents under a candidate allowlist and find what breaks. Start from the 80 variables the denylist currently keeps on this machine — a real sample rather than a guess. Watch SSH_AUTH_SOCK in particular; the denylist already had to make an exception for it.

tasks.title: Voice connector intermittently reports 'server isn't responding' on dispatch_to_agent and message_agent
tasks.done_when: Either a cause is identified and fixed, or the intermittent failure is shown to be client-side and the finding written down so it is not re-investigated
tasks.notes:
Filed by the voice agent as relay item 192: hit several times during the item 185/186 phone session, succeeding on retry.

Not yet reproduced or diagnosed. Worth noting what is already known before spending time on it:

- Both named verbs WRITE, and both do more work than the reads: dispatch_to_agent does getItem + updateItem, message_agent does getItem + a kind-filtered listEvents + appendEvent.
- The Worker's audit trail should show whether the request arrived at all. If there is no audit row, the failure is between the connector and Cloudflare and relay never saw it; if there is one with a 5xx, it is relay's. That single check decides which half to investigate and costs one query against audit_log.
- Cold start is plausible but unproven — the Worker startup time reported at deploy was 48ms, which argues against it.

Deliberately low priority until that first audit_log check is done, because it decides whether there is anything here to fix at all.

tasks.title: Schedule the index-drift detector — it is the only unassessable flip trigger
tasks.done_when: The 49ms drift detector runs on a defined schedule, its result is recorded somewhere durable, and flip trigger 3 in deepdive-storage-decision.md §6 has an evidence-based verdict rather than "no data either way".
tasks.notes:
Split out of R-33 2026-07-27.

`deepdive-storage-decision.md` §6 lists four flip triggers for moving off D1. As
of 2026-07-27, triggers 1, 2 and 4 were re-assessed against the larger expected
corpus and are **not tripped**. Trigger 3 — "a demonstrated instance of index
drift from an out-of-band write in normal operation" — is the only one that is
**unassessable**, because nobody has ever run the detector on a schedule.

The decision doc itself proposed exactly this: "answerable by running the 49 ms
detector on a schedule and seeing whether it ever fires."

## Why it matters more than its size suggests

Index drift is the **one genuine, unfixable-on-D1 defect** identified in the whole
storage reassessment. Postgres can declare `tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS` so drift
cannot happen; SQLite-on-D1 cannot, so postings maintenance lives in application
code and any out-of-band write desynchronises the index silently. **Detection is
the only available mitigation.**

If it ever fires, the defect moves from theoretical to observed and structural
prevention becomes worth a server — i.e. this cheap ticket is the deciding
evidence for a much larger decision.

## Where it goes

`docs/scheduled-maintenance.md` and the existing maintenance infrastructure from
R-16. 49 ms, so cost is not a consideration. The only real design question is
where a firing result gets recorded so it is not lost in logs.

## A SECOND DETECTOR NOW EXISTS — schedule them together (added 2026-07-28)

R-41 shipped `scripts/check-schema-drift.sh` and closed. It detects a DIFFERENT
drift — the live SCHEMA versus baseline+migrations, not the FTS index versus
items — but it lands on exactly the same open design question as this ticket,
and it lands there for exactly the same reason.

  make check-drift-remote     # read-only against production, ~seconds

Both are cheap detectors whose value is entirely in being run repeatedly and
having a firing recorded somewhere that is not a log line. Neither is scheduled.
CI cannot cover either one against a real database: CI holds no Cloudflare token
by design, and for schema drift a CI run is a tautology anyway (CI builds its
database from the same chain the check compares against — see the comment in
the schema-drift job).

So whatever this ticket decides about WHERE a firing gets durably recorded
should be decided once and applied to both. Solving it twice, differently, is
the likely failure mode.

Worth noting the asymmetry when designing the record: schema drift firing means
a deploy path is broken and is actionable immediately. Index drift firing is
EVIDENCE FOR A STORAGE MIGRATION — it needs to survive long enough to be cited
in a decision months later, which is a stronger durability requirement than an
alert.

Baseline as of 2026-07-28: production schema is clean, 22 objects, no drift.
That is the first time it has been checked rather than assumed.

## BLOCKED 2026-07-30 — premise does not hold, no detector can be built yet

Investigated to implement this ticket and found the premise is false: **there is
no hand-rolled BM25/postings implementation in the codebase to check for drift
against.** deepdive-storage-decision.md itself is future tense about it ("When
full-text search arrives it will be hand-rolled BM25 over ordinary tables" —
§1), and that has not happened. Verified by grep across worker/src and
worker/migrations: zero matches for postings/term-stats/tokenizer/bm25 tables or
maintenance code. R-21 ("storage module seam + D1 compatibility CI") shipped and
is marked done, but it only delivered the seam/CI-export guardrails — the actual
hand-rolled indexer described in the same doc's §3 benchmarks was never built.

The only related artifact is `items.indexed_at` (schema comment: "search-index
drift" placeholder, backed by partial index `idx_items_stale`). It is set to
NULL on every insert (worker/src/items.ts) and is **never written anywhere else
in the codebase** — nothing ever transitions it off NULL. There is no
source-of-truth recompute function and no actual index to compare it against.

Consequence: a "recompute-and-assert" detector has nothing real to recompute.
Built today it would either always report "0 items indexed, no drift possible"
(vacuous — provides no evidence for trigger 3 either way) or flag every row as
"never indexed" (not drift, just the absence of the feature). Neither produces
the evidence-based verdict this ticket's done_when asks for. A check that
reports something meaningless erodes trust in every other check the same way a
false positive would.

R-37 as scoped is **blocked on a prerequisite that doesn't exist**: the BM25
postings feature itself. Escalated to the operator 2026-07-30 for a scoping
decision (defer this ticket / narrow it to a tautological indexed_at-bookkeeping
check / build the missing indexer first) before any implementation proceeds.
No code was written against this ticket.

Split out of the probe 4 Part B debugging on 2026-07-28. See plan doc §2.7.

  GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
    -> 200 {"resource": "https://relay.hjewkes.workers.dev", ...}
  GET https://relay.hjewkes.workers.dev
    -> 404

The per-path document is correct and is the one that matters:
/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp/admin names
"https://relay.hjewkes.workers.dev/mcp/admin", and the 401 from /mcp/admin
points at it via WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata. That path is what a
spec-compliant client follows, and it works.

## NOT A BUG WE HIT — read this before spending time on it

This was hypothesis (2) for why the admin verbs would not attach on
2026-07-28. It was WRONG. The real cause was createMcpHandler's default
route (fixed in 9fba48d). Fixing this document would not have attached a
single tool. It is filed low priority precisely so it is not mistaken for
a live defect.

Why it is still worth doing eventually: the root document is emitted by
@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider as a generic fallback; relay never asked
for it and does not serve anything at the origin. An advertisement pointing
at a 404 is a false signal that will mislead the next person debugging a
discovery problem — it already cost part of one session.

Check first whether the library lets the root document be suppressed or its
resource overridden. If it does not, decide deliberately between serving
something meaningful at the origin and accepting the noise with a comment,
rather than patching around the library.

tasks.title: Replace BM25 ∪ recency candidate generation with a 1-bit sign sketch
tasks.done_when: Candidate generation for relay's search uses a 1-bit sign sketch with exact float32 rerank, and its recall is re-measured on relay's OWN items with relay's OWN embedding model rather than extrapolated from the brain corpus.
tasks.notes:
## Falls directly out of R-22. Evidence: docs/hybrid-search-recall.md.
## NOT urgent — relay has no search yet. This is the design to build WHEN it does.

R-22 measured the currently-designed candidate generator against 16,705 real
vectors and 1,763 queries. It is the weakest link, and the replacement is cheap
and needs no change of database.

  BM25 union recency, N=100        55.8% recall@10 vs exact float32
    - the recency arm alone         1.6%  — near-worthless as a semantic source
    - to reach 92%                  must scan ~30% of the corpus
  1-bit sign sketch, N=100         96.6% recall@10, at 48 BYTES PER VECTOR
    - on the hardest queries        93.3% vs 35.6% for BM25 union recency

## THE TWO CHEAP WINS, both measured (§6b)
1. KEEP THE QUERY IN FLOAT32 rather than binarising it. Worth more than the
   threshold choice and costs NOTHING in storage, because the query is never
   stored. Binarised query: 0.873 @K=100. Float32 query: 0.966.
2. Mean-centred threshold is worth ~18 points ONLY IF the query is also
   binarised (0.873 vs 0.692). With a float32 query the threshold barely matters
   (0.966 vs 0.961). So do #1 and the threshold decision becomes low-stakes.

int8 is effectively lossless if exactness is ever needed: 0.997 @K=20, 1.000
from K=100. Costs 4x the bytes of the 1-bit sketch.

## WHAT MUST BE RE-MEASURED BEFORE TRUSTING THESE NUMBERS HERE
R-22's numbers come from BRAIN CHUNKS (250-1800 chars), not relay items, using
bge-small-en-v1.5 (384d) and nomic-embed-text (768d) — neither of which is
necessarily relay's model. Two extrapolations to check:
- SHORTER DOCUMENTS. Relay items are shorter than brain chunks. Sparser term
  statistics generally make BM25 WORSE, so the comparison should if anything
  favour the sketch more — but that is reasoning, not measurement.
- SMALLER CORPUS. Recall at fixed N improves as the corpus shrinks. R-22 reports
  N as a percentage of corpus precisely so this can be re-derived.

## DO NOT CITE recall@10 ALONE
It measures agreement with a vector-search ORACLE — "is this a faithful
approximation of exact vector search?" That is the R-21 question, not the
quality question. R-22's §5 measures quality oracle-free (does the pipeline
return the chunk the query was written from) and points the OTHER WAY: hybrid
0.594 vs exact float32 0.557. Both must be reported together.

## SEQUENCING
Not blocking anything. relay has no search surface today and the v0 inbox does
not need one. Build this when search is actually built, and re-measure first.

tasks.title: R2 blob tier: D1 holds metadata and a reference, R2 holds the bytes
tasks.done_when: relay can store and retrieve a binary larger than D1's 2MB row limit, with the D1 row holding key/size/content-type/etag and R2 holding the bytes; the write ordering and orphan-sweep behaviour on partial failure is a written, tested decision; and the 10,000-char body cap has been resolved one way or the other for large TEXT.
tasks.notes:
Split out of R-33 2026-07-27. R-33 decided the ATTRIBUTE model; this is the
storage-tier gap it exposed. See docs/attribute-model.md.

## Why this is now due

relay has NO object storage configured. Measured against the two corpora it is
expected to hold:

- logan: 412 files, ~1.47 GB, **99.85% binary**. **46 files exceed D1's 2 MB row
  limit**, largest 566 MB. R2's 5 TiB object ceiling covers it comfortably.
- Cloudflare's own guidance is "never store files in D1" — a stated design
  position, not merely a size workaround.

## Two separate problems, do not conflate them

1. **Binaries** — genuinely need R2. Non-negotiable.
2. **Large TEXT** — a different problem with a different fix. **159 of
   active-work's 913 documents exceed relay's 10,000-char `body` cap** (largest
   186,728 chars), plus 28 of logan's text files (largest 1,022,371 chars). But
   **ZERO exceed D1's 2 MB row limit.** So the binding constraint is relay's own
   application-level cap, not the database. Decide whether to raise the cap or
   move full text to R2 — do not assume the latter.

Useful finding for (2): hybrid search operates on CHUNKS, not whole documents, in
every production pattern researched. So moving full text to R2 does NOT break
BM25 or vector retrieval. It costs one extra fetch on the show-whole-document
path. That makes it a real option rather than a compromise.

## The hard part

`db.batch()` is atomic but obviously cannot span R2. **No Cloudflare-documented
cross-system consistency or cleanup mechanism exists** for the D1-write/R2-write
split — the researched "write R2 first, then sweep orphans" pattern was inference
from each system's individually-documented properties, NOT a citation. Treat it
as a design decision to make and test, not a pattern to copy.

## Gated on

Do not ingest logan until the data-handling ticket closes. The corpus contains
wire instructions, escrow and closing disclosures, mortgage and insurance
documents, title records and security footage.

tasks.title: Entities as first-class rows: vendors and people graduate out of the agenda tag
tasks.done_when: A vendor or person is a real row referenced by edges rather than a tag value, a document can reference more than one, and the existing agenda tag values are migrated onto it with the person-vs-organization distinction preserved.
tasks.notes:
## SEQUENCING, 2026-07-28: reference content (R-40) goes FIRST.

R-38's notes proposed entities as the next type because they are what tests the
registry's keying dimension. The operator chose otherwise, for a good reason:
being able to take and look up non-task notes is a capability relay does not
have at all, whereas entities improve something that already works.

That ordering is fine and changes nothing here — but note the one thing it
defers. The `type_schemas` registry was deliberately keyed on `kind` rather than
scoped to items SO THAT entities could register in it without a retrofit
(Paperless-ngx scoped its equivalent to documents only and has years of
unresolved requests to widen it). That decision is now UNTESTED until this
ticket lands. Nothing is lost by waiting; just do not let R-39's tool
autogeneration harden around item-shaped kinds only.

---

Split out of R-33 2026-07-27. See docs/attribute-model.md §5.

Plan doc §6 deferred "an `entities` table (`vendor:` graduates first)". The
condition it was waiting for has arrived.

## Vendor cannot be a scalar attribute — this is the decisive finding

logan contains real **multi-vendor documents** (referrals, subcontractor
pass-through bids). So vendor is a RELATIONSHIP, not a column and not a meta key.
Paperless-ngx — the closest analogue found, a scanned-document archive — models
Correspondent as a real FK'd table rather than a tag, independently confirming
this.

## The agenda tag is NOT a clean proto-entity table

An earlier read of this was wrong and the mapping is messier than it looks:

- `liaison`, `murphy-door` — match logan directories directly
- `sundown` -> `dbs`, `thorne-french` -> `tf-renovations` — match vendor DBA
  names, not logan's own slugs
- **`conrad` is a PERSON** (Conrad Hall at hall-marble), not a vendor
- `allen` is a friend, not a vendor at all
- `cole` matches nothing in logan

So `agenda` means "people to raise things with", conflating individuals and
organizations. **The design must model both, plus the person-to-org
relationship.** A straight rename of the tag namespace will not do.

Other vendors present in logan but absent from relay: kaleidoscope, shed,
affordable-flooring, california-closets, dan-maloney, great-western, ken-caryl,
smart-choice, plus ~10 one-offs.

## Registry keying — decide up front, do not retrofit

Paperless-ngx scoped its CustomField system to Documents only and has years of
unresolved requests (#10826 and others) to extend it to Correspondents and
DocumentTypes. **R-33's `type_schemas` registry must key on entities from the
start.** This surfaced twice independently in the research; it is the most
predictable trap here.

## New relation types needed

All INSERTs into `relation_types`, no schema change: `supersedes`, `invoices`,
`attached-to`, `cites`. Real demand exists — a documented chain in logan (bid ->
revised signed bid -> invoice, plus a change order explicitly marked superseded),
47 superseded docs in active-work with multi-hop chains, and 1,345 wikilinks.

Also worth carrying: `cites-external` (URL + type + accessed-date) is NOT an
item-to-item edge and needs a different home.

tasks.title: Audit the OAuth door: the trail is built and wired — three paths have never fired in production
tasks.done_when:
Four OAuth paths are each observed writing their audit_log row against
production, not just unit-tested: a successful authorization (DONE
2026-07-28), an allowlist rejection carrying the rejected login as actor, a
state/callback rejection with actor=null, and a revocation. Plus: no row in

tasks.notes:
REVISED 2026-07-28. The original problem statement is obsolete and was
actively misleading: it said the OAuth door "produces NOTHING". It produces
five event types, four of them from named builders in `worker/src/audit.ts`.
The implementation work is done. **What is left is production verification.**

Discovered while running probe 4 Part B (R-23), which caused two of these
rows to be written and observed.

## Actual state

| Event | Wired at | Fired in prod? |
|---|---|---|
| Authorization granted | `github-handler.ts:252` | YES — 2 rows, 2026-07-28 |
| Token issued/refreshed | `index.ts:137` (`tokenExchangeCallback`) | YES — 14 rows since 2026-07-27 |
| Rate-limit denial on `/authorize` | `index.ts:183` | YES — 4 rows, but this is R-9's, not R-19's |
| **Allowlist rejection** | `github-handler.ts:223` | **NEVER** |
| **State / callback rejection** | `github-handler.ts:182` | **NEVER** |
| **Revocation** | `scripts/revoke-oauth-access.sh:87` | **NEVER** |

Two things the original ticket did not anticipate:

- **State/callback rejection was built anyway** (`oauthStateRejected`), beyond
  the ticket's four events. It is unverified, so it is now in the gate — an
  implemented-but-never-exercised security path is exactly what rots.
- **Revocation cannot be observed by the Worker.** `wrangler kv bulk delete`
  talks to the KV API directly, so no request reaches us. The script writes its
  own row instead. See the comment at `audit.ts:176`. If revocation ever moves
  behind a Worker route, the row belongs back in `audit.ts` with the others.

The decision about recording the rejected GitHub login was already made and
documented at length at `audit.ts:81-99` — it is recorded deliberately, because
"someone was rejected" without "who" cannot tell one persistent prober from ten
passers-by. No need to re-litigate it.

## What is left

- [ ] Verify **allowlist rejection** writes `door=oauth action=authorize
      outcome=denied` with `actor=<rejected login>`. Needs a second GitHub
      account — same method R-18 used. NOTE: R-18 verified the *denial
      behaviour* on 2026-07-26, before this builder existed, which is why there
      is no row from that run.
- [ ] Verify **state/callback rejection** writes `door=oauth action=callback
      outcome=denied`, `actor=null`, and that the state token is absent from
      `detail`.
- [ ] Verify **revocation** writes `door=oauth action=revoke outcome=ok`.
- [ ] Confirm no row in any path carries `state`, an authorization code, or
      token material.
- [ ] Update `docs/security-posture.md`, which still lists this as an
      unmitigated gap.

## SEQUENCING — do not trip over this

Do **not** run the revocation verification until R-23's probe 4 Part B is
settled. Revoking destroys the `relay-admin` grant issued 2026-07-28T14:18:11Z,
which Part B still needs in order to finish its attribution check.

## Watch out

Unchanged and still binding: never log the OAuth state parameter, the
authorization code, or any token material. A row says WHO and WHAT HAPPENED,
never WITH WHAT CREDENTIAL.

tasks.title: active-work convergence: relay as the backing store, not a second copy
tasks.done_when: A decision is written down on whether active-work reads and writes tasks through relay rather than keeping its own copy, with the seam identified and the migration path costed. Design only — no implementation until R-20 and R-27 close.
tasks.notes:
## DESIGN ONLY. Raised by the operator 2026-07-27 off the back of items 101-108.
## Charter-confirming, not charter-changing — but now with a concrete mechanism.

relay's README already states the direction: brain, active-work and herald
"incrementally and carefully converge INTO it, and are eventually subsumed."
This ticket exists because the convergence stopped being abstract.

## THE EVIDENCE — this session demonstrated the problem while working
The phone filed relay items 101-108 (feedback on relay itself). Triaging them,
this session COPIED THEM INTO ACTIVE-WORK as R-27, R-28, R-29 and R-30. Same
content, two stores, hand-transcribed by an agent, already diverging: the
active-work copies carry a corrected diagnosis for item 107 that the relay item
does not, and relay items 101/102/103/108 are "closed as already-built" only in
the active-work copy.

That is the copying the operator named, observed live. Also note R-25 imported
98 items from Drive into relay while the same backlog lives in active-work, and
this session's own bootstrap prompt was assembled from active-work while relay
holds the operator's real inbox.

## WHY IT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS R-26
active-work is a local filesystem store with an MCP daemon on 127.0.0.1:7400.
agent-chat is a local SQLite store with a broker on a unix socket. BOTH converge
on relay by the SAME seam: durable state moves to the cloud, ephemeral/local
concerns (process spawning, live sockets, filesystem worktrees) stay local.
Design them together or they will grow two different answers to one question.
See docs/agent-orchestration.md.

## WHAT MAKES THIS HARDER THAN agent-chat
- active-work's structure is RICHER than relay's items: brief, handoff, tasks,
  sessions, artifacts, sources, worktrees. relay has items/tags/edges. Either
  relay grows those concepts or active-work keeps a local layer above relay.
- active-work is OFFLINE-CRITICAL in a way chat is not. Bootstrapping a session
  on a plane must work. Same unresolved question as R-26 open question 3.
- active-work's CLI writes are the validation boundary ("edits route through the
  CLI"). Moving storage to relay must not move validation to the Worker — relay's
  own rule is that storage methods are persistence only, with policy in the
  domain modules.
- PREREQUISITE: R-29. Today every relay dev ticket is area='projects', so relay
  cannot distinguish its own backlog from Voltras or Logan Street. A backing
  store that cannot separate initiatives cannot back active-work at all.

## DO NOT START THIS BEFORE
R-20 (token scope — this widens what a compromised token reaches), R-27 (admin
surface reachable, or there is no way to maintain the data), and R-29 (project
entity). Sequenced behind all three deliberately.

## THE PRINCIPLE THAT CONSTRAINS IT
relay's charter: spin-off primitives "only ever become libraries if they never
grow tendrils into relay's internals." The inverse applies here — active-work
must consume relay through a published interface, not reach into its D1 schema.
A convergence that couples them at the schema is not convergence, it is a merge
that can never be undone.

tasks.title: Data minimization and retention policy
tasks.done_when: relay stores no field it does not use, has a written rule for what must never be put in it, and old rows are purged on a defined schedule.
tasks.notes:
## STATUS 2026-07-27: MINIMIZATION DONE, PURGE TOOL DONE, REPORT SCHEDULED,
## APPLY DELIBERATELY NOT AUTOMATED. THIS TICKET DOES NOT CLOSE YET.

DONE earlier (do not redo): `email` removed from Props (R-6); `accessToken`
removed and GitHub scope narrowed to empty (R-15); two log leaks fixed; README
opens with "What relay must never hold"; `audit_log` purge tooling shipped
(scripts/audit-purge.sh, worker/sql/audit-purge-preview.sql read-only BY
CONSTRUCTION with a test asserting it contains no mutating statement, and
audit-purge-apply.sql). Dry-run is the DEFAULT; `--apply` is required.
WINDOW: 90 days, argued not picked — 3x the 30-day D1 Time Travel window, so for
any restorable database state the audit rows explaining it still exist. Also
matches the 90-day default daemon token lifetime. Argument against longer: an
allowlist rejection records the GitHub login of whoever was rejected, so the
table slowly accumulates identities of people who are not relay's user.

## 2026-07-27 — THE TTY TENSION WAS NOT WEAKENED. Read this before "fixing" it.
scripts/audit-purge.sh refuses a `--remote` delete it cannot get interactive
confirmation for, and a test asserts it aborts non-zero on `--remote --apply`
without a TTY. Automating the purge conflicts with that guard ON PURPOSE.

RESOLUTION SHIPPED: the scheduled job runs the PREVIEW (read-only by
construction) and ALERTS on the first night purgeable > 0, naming the exact
command to run. Verified: no `--apply` appears anywhere in
scripts/relay-maintenance.sh.

THE REASONING, which is the part worth keeping: the guard protects "every
production deletion is a human decision." What manual-only ACTUALLY fails at is
nobody looking — and only that is fixed here. The decisive fact is that NO
APPLIED RUN AGAINST PRODUCTION HAS EVER HAPPENED, and audit_log does not cross
90 days until ~late Oct 2026. So automating now would ship a delete path whose
FIRST REAL EXECUTION IS UNATTENDED. That is the wrong order.

## WHY THIS TICKET STAYS OPEN
done_when says "old rows are purged on a defined schedule." A scheduled REPORT
is not a scheduled PURGE. The promotion checklist is in
docs/scheduled-maintenance.md — promote the apply only after at least one
watched manual run against production has succeeded.

Also outstanding: the LaunchAgent is WRITTEN BUT NOT INSTALLED (verified —
`launchctl list` shows no relay job), so even the report is not yet running. See
R-16, which shares the script, the host decision and the alerting requirement.

## ITEM RETENTION — still deliberately not designed
`items` now exists (R-2 shipped), so the seam marked in the purge script is
reachable. But a retention rule for the operator's actual inbox is a different
question from audit rows and should not be inherited from the 90-day window
without an argument. R-26 notes that a high-volume agent event log would make
this urgent rather than theoretical.

tasks.title: Prompt-injection hardening for the agent runner
tasks.done_when: Item content reaching a headless Claude session is structurally marked as untrusted data, and the runner's capabilities are constrained such that a hostile item cannot escalate beyond an allowlisted workspace.
tasks.notes:
## STATUS 2026-07-26 — THREAT MODEL DONE, IMPLEMENTATION NOT STARTED (f619b9d, merged)

SHIPPED: docs/agent-runner-threat-model.md (718 lines). Sections: assets; trust
boundaries; auth state before/after R-6; 15 enumerated threats (T1-T15); mitigations
tiered by strength; human-in-the-loop boundary; residual risk; red-team test plan.

Threats it surfaced that the original ticket missed:
- T3 instruction laundering through fetched content
- T7 argv/environment injection into the spawn call itself
- T14 status/event reporting as an injection channel aimed back at the OPERATOR
  when they read results
- T11 missing atomic claim -> duplicate execution
- T13 cursor / poll-loop manipulation

Sharper framings worth carrying into implementation:
- `--allowed-tools` bounds what is TYPED, not what is REACHABLE. If any interpreter
  is permitted (node, python, make, npm run), assume general shell capability.
- TOCTOU on path containment: realpath is checked at spawn, but a symlink created
  mid-session escapes it. Unfixable without OS-level sandboxing or a VM.
- Egress restriction is UNVERIFIED: could not confirm a Seatbelt profile or any
  per-process network restriction works with `claude -p` on macOS 26.5.1. Documented
  as the largest known gap, not as a solved mitigation.

OUTSTANDING — why this ticket is still open. NONE of the code exists:
1. Path allowlist w/ realpath + containment check, unit tested against traversal
   payloads ('../', symlinks, absolute paths).
2. Untrusted-data prompt wrapper, unit tested against delimiter injection.
3. Explicit --allowed-tools + wall-clock timeout enforced in the spawn call.
4. Human-in-the-loop gate for push/deploy/irreversible actions.
5. Red-team execution: write the hostile items from the doc's §8 test plan, confirm
   each is blocked, record results back into the doc.

This is a HARD DEPENDENCY of R-3 and cannot be closed until R-3's runner exists to
harden. Consider doing 1-4 as part of R-3 rather than before it.

## CODE DONE 2026-07-27. NOT CLOSED — the job is written but NOT INSTALLED.
## Docs: docs/scheduled-maintenance.md. Scripts: scripts/relay-maintenance.sh,

manual action." The plist exists; nothing is loaded. Verified: `launchctl list`
shows no relay job. THE OPERATOR MUST INSTALL IT — see the doc.

## HOST — decided and argued
Standalone launchd LaunchAgent `com.relay.maintenance`, using
StartCalendarInterval, NOT KeepAlive. KeepAlive would relaunch a job that runs a
minute and exits — i.e. export production continuously in a loop. A calendar
interval also runs a missed job after the laptop wakes rather than skipping it,
which is the behaviour a backup wants.
R-3 does not exist yet. When it does, its right role is WATCHING this job, not
hosting it.

free today and exists before it becomes load-bearing. Tested both ways.

## ENCRYPTION — decided
`age` to a PUBLIC recipient: the job writes archives it cannot read back, and the
identity lives off-laptop. Missing recipients is a HARD FAILURE, never a silent
fallback to plaintext.
`make db-export-remote` stays plaintext deliberately — you need it readable
during a restore — but now carries a 7-day leash.

## RETENTION — decided
90d encrypted (matches R-12's audit_log window), 7d plaintext, and a FLOOR OF 7
ARCHIVES so a laptop closed for a season cannot prune itself to zero.
Documented honestly: worst-case row lifetime is ~180d, not 90.

tasks.done_when: items.area is replaced by a real project entity (R-35-pattern: first-class row, not an item), carrying its own status/due date/description; items reference it via an edge or FK. Migration creates 4 seed projects (Home, Health, Admin, Projects) and backfills every existing item's project reference from its old area value, then drops the area column. tasks.notes:
CORRECTED 2026-07-30, same session, after the original design below was found to conflict with pre-existing research (R-33's docs/attribute-model.md §7 and docs/project-entity-options.md) that this design session didn't check first.

## Corrected direction
Per docs/attribute-model.md §7: project is either a registered `meta` attribute or an entity with edges — never a tag namespace, never a `kind='project'` item. Re-asked the operator the memo's deciding question directly: does a project need its own data (status, due date, description)? Answer: YES. That selects the entity-with-edges branch, which per R-33's own framing (and R-35's "vendors are a relationship, not an attribute... entities get real rows and edges") means project should be a REAL ENTITY ROW, coordinated with R-35 ("entities as first-class rows"), not an item with kind='project'. The original design below built project as an item — that part is superseded.

Operator also re-confirmed REPLACING area entirely (not nesting under it, which is what docs/project-entity-options.md itself recommends and argues for at length — Voltras/Logan Street would otherwise both stay area='projects', just different projects). This was asked explicitly a second time, after surfacing the memo's counter-argument, and the operator held the original answer. Treat as a deliberate override of the memo's recommendation, not an oversight.

## Still true from the original design (unaffected by the correction)
- Flat, freely-created — no separate CRUD step, a project is created by naming it.
- Voice capture fuzzy-matches a spoken project name against existing ones, reads back the match before creating a new one.
- Migration backfills existing items' area value into 4 seed projects (Home, Health, Admin, Projects).

## Superseded by this correction
- "Modeled as items + relations" (decision 3 in the original notes) — no. Project is an entity row, not an item.
- The exact schema (project_item_id self-referential FK on items) — no longer applies; the entity's own table/columns and the item→project reference shape need to be designed jointly with R-35, not invented separately here.

## Relationship to other tickets
- Supersedes relay backlog item #105 (design conversation was the blocker; now unblocked).
- Supersedes/absorbs R-29 (same problem, filed 2026-07-27, referenced this same R-33/R-35 context that this session initially missed). R-29 should be closed as done/superseded once this task is filed correctly — do not run both.
- MUST be coordinated with R-35 ("entities as first-class rows: vendors and people graduate out of the agenda tag") — R-29's own notes say if project becomes an entity it should be designed alongside vendors and people, not separately. Whether project shares R-35's entities table (with a type discriminator) or gets its own table is an open question for that joint design, not decided here.
- docs/project-entity-options.md's Option 3 (dedicated `projects` table + FK) is now the closest-fitting of its three options, given "needs its own data" — but should still be reconciled against whatever R-35 designs for vendors/people rather than built as a fourth, unrelated entity shape.

## Open implementation questions (unresolved, no planning pass done — brain MCP not connected this session)
- Whether project is its own table or a row in a shared R-35 entities table with a type/kind discriminator.
- Exact columns beyond name: status, due date, description were named as wanted; full schema undesigned.
- How items reference a project (edge vs FK) — should match whatever R-35 picks for vendor/person references, for consistency.
- Exact voice tool schema changes for mcp-tools.ts and admin-tools.ts (currently z.enum(ITEM_AREAS) in both).
- Fuzzy-match algorithm and confidence threshold for voice capture.
- Interaction with R-42 (presence + nullable split) — is the project reference required-and-nullable or plain optional?

---

## Original design (2026-07-30, pre-correction, kept for history)

Design settled via brainstorming skill on 2026-07-30, operator-approved section by section.

Motivation (operator, concrete case): the 'projects' area bucket is too coarse. Breaking general projects into individual initiatives, spinning up new initiatives more specific than the four area buckets, planning work items, planning trips — all need an extra level of organization beyond the fixed 4-value area enum.

Key decisions, each explicitly chosen by the operator over an alternative:
1. Flat, freely-created (not hierarchical, not tied 1:1 to active-work initiative slugs) — a project is just a name, created by saying/writing it, no separate CRUD step.
2. Replaces area entirely, not an additional field alongside it.
3. [SUPERSEDED, see above] Modeled as items + relations, not a dedicated standalone table — a project is kind='project', an ordinary item. Other items point at it via a new item_item relation (project_item_id). Chosen deliberately as a first mover for relay's stated 'not yet, never not ever' relations seam, reusing voice capture / listing / notes / status machinery that already exists for items rather than building a second parallel entity system.

tasks.title: Add append-only comments to items (relay item #138 design)
tasks.done_when: items gets an array-valued attribute at meta.comments ([{time, text}], append-only), registered in type_schemas per R-33's attribute model (not a bespoke comments_json column); a new dedicated voice tool add_comment(item_id, text) appends one entry with a confirm-gated readback matching complete_item/update_item's pattern; admin surface gets an equivalent.
tasks.notes:
CORRECTED 2026-07-31, after realizing R-33 (docs/attribute-model.md) already establishes a single validated `meta` JSON column, registered per-kind in `type_schemas`, as the mechanism for exactly this kind of type-specific data. A bespoke comments_json column would be a second, parallel JSON mechanism duplicating that pattern rather than using it — caught while reconciling R-51/#105 against R-33, and the operator confirmed the same correction applies here.

Comments now live at meta.comments (an array-valued attribute, registered in type_schemas), not a separate column. The append-only semantics (comments are pushed, never rewritten) are an application-layer rule enforced by add_comment, same as elsewhere in the codebase — R-33 doesn't require every meta attribute to be scalar, and "array of {time,text}, append-only" is a legitimate attribute shape under that model.

Original notes preserved below (storage mechanism superseded; everything else still applies).

---

Design settled via brainstorming skill on 2026-07-30, operator-approved section by section.

Motivation: want partial-status updates on a task — notes that relate to and live with that task over time, not full item mutations.

Key decisions:
1. Dedicated voice tool (add_comment), not an added param on update_item — keeps update_item's confirmation readback simple, gives comments their own singular confirm string. This is the 7th voice verb.
2. [SUPERSEDED, see above] Storage: comments_json array column on items, NOT a comment-as-item relation. Explicit operator choice against the relation-reuse pattern for this case — this is deliberately relay's first meta_json-style column, an exception to the brief's 'not yet' list, made consciously rather than by default. (Turned out relay already has a meta-JSON mechanism via R-33; comments now use it rather than inventing a second one.)

tasks.title: [AW-h] Wire @titan-design/memory into wrap and open
tasks.done_when: wrap curates deltas from what the session recorded; open recalls scoped to the initiative plus global; reflection deterministic by default with model-driven opt-in, matching TP-19's shape in session-miner
tasks.notes:
CORRECTED 2026-09-10 by kg-vision, verified against the code before accepting.

As filed this item was WRONG. The recompose doc §2 said put the initiative slug in memory's `scope`. That cannot work and would invert the goal:
  packages/memory/src/types.ts:8   BULLET_SCOPES = ['global','workspace','language','framework','task'] — closed
  packages/memory/src/types.ts:106 scope: z.enum(BULLET_SCOPES).default('workspace') — a slug fails validation
  packages/memory/src/recall.ts:72 inScope() returns scope === undefined || bullet.scope === 'global' || bullet.scope === scope
So a slug is rejected today, and if the enum were widened to accept one, recall would HIDE every bullet from every other initiative — the exact opposite of an initiative whose point is cross-initiative reuse.

Use tags to carry the initiative. `scope`'s default 'workspace' already means the whole active root, which is the right granularity.

Second correction from the same review: tags alone cannot carry cross-initiative knowledge. 367 of 419 tags appear in exactly one initiative, and body mentions reach about twice the initiatives that tags do (worktree 8 vs 3, daemon 7 vs 3, vitest 4 vs 0). Retrieval has to read bodies, not just tag metadata.

See sources/design-knowledge-graph.md before implementing this.

tasks.title: Open-loop ledger rejects resolution by session id, so a reused id can never close its own loops
tasks.done_when: a later session file can resolve a loop opened by an earlier file that shares its session_id; the 33 accumulated loops in titan-platform can be closed; a regression test covers two files with one id
tasks.notes:
Found 2026-09-10 while wrapping. src/sessions/open-loops.ts:282 rejects a resolve when the target loop's session_id equals the resolving session's, regardless of which FILE opened it:

  if (target.session.sessionId === session.sessionId) return 'self';

Claude Code reuses a session_id across days, so a long-running id can never close any loop it ever opened. Measured in titan-platform today: 33 open loops accumulated across 2026-09-08 to 2026-09-10 under one id, 14 of them demonstrably done (npm bootstrap, first CI publish, agent worktrees, the TaskResolver seam, the cli-reference decision, the migrations guard, and more). wrap reported all 14 as resolves_rejected with kind 'self' and applied zero.

The guard is broader than its own justification. Its comment cites pickAvailableFilename parking a colliding record at <stem>-1.md, so a self-directed resolve could land on the earlier file and close a different record's live loop. But line 279 already rejects the same session FILE, and line 283's endedMs comparison already blocks the mutual-close cycle. Line 282 adds only the case where two different files, days apart, share an id — which is legitimate and is the common case for this workspace.

Proposed fix: drop the session_id equality check and rely on the file check plus the endedMs ordering. If the pickAvailableFilename hazard is real, narrow the guard to that specific shape (same id AND same stem family) rather than all shared ids.

Regression test: two session files, different stems, same session_id, the later ending after the earlier. The later must be able to resolve the earlier's loop. There is an existing suite in __tests__/sessions/ for the ledger.

Worth doing before the ledger becomes useless: it is the mechanism the bootstrap uses to show what is still hanging, and 33 stale entries is already past the point where an operator reads it.

One correction that came with this: the ledger does NOT fail silently, contrary to the note filed 2026-09-09. wrap returns resolves_rejected naming every refused ref and its reason. That note is corrected in place.

tasks.title: A release can be tagged on a commit that does not carry its own version
tasks.done_when: One command takes active-work from a merged feature branch to a published release: it merges the version PR, refuses to tag unless the checked-out commit's package.json matches the tag, then tags and pushes. Tagging a mismatched commit is impossible rather than merely discouraged.
tasks.notes:
Hit 2026-09-11 on the 0.6.0 release, caught before the workflow ran.

The release is tag-triggered and the workflow validates that the tag matches package.json — so a mismatch fails CI rather than publishing something wrong. The exposure is that the check is at the END of a manual sequence: open a version PR, wait for checks, merge, pull, tag, push. Tagging before the merge lands puts the tag on a commit whose package.json still says the old version, and you only learn on the next CI run.

WHAT HAPPENED: `gh pr merge 126` reported BLOCKED because required status check `check` had not started yet, but the same shell line went on to tag and push. v0.6.0 landed on 4d20341, where package.json said 0.5.0. Deleted the tag, waited for the check, merged, re-tagged on de3bf13. No bad publish.

CONTRIBUTING CAUSE, which is the more general lesson: my wait loop was `until [ "$(gh pr view N --json statusCheckRollup -q '[.statusCheckRollup[]|select(.status!="COMPLETED")]|length')" = "0" ]`. An EMPTY rollup satisfies that immediately — zero incomplete checks is also zero checks. GitHub populates the rollup a few seconds after the push, so polling too early exits at once. The correct predicate counts COMPLETED checks and requires at least one. This affected three releases today; two got lucky.

SUGGESTED SHAPE: a `scripts/release.mjs` that takes the version, opens or finds the release PR, waits on at least one completed required check, merges, pulls, asserts `require('./package.json').version === tag.slice(1)` against the FRESH checkout, then tags. The assertion is the point; the automation is just what makes the assertion unskippable.

Not urgent — the workflow's own version check is the real backstop, and it works. This removes a step where a human has to be careful instead.

tasks.title: wrap: a second wrap in one session orphans the loops the first one filed
tasks.done_when: wrapping twice in one session either updates the existing session record, or lets the second wrap resolve loops the first one filed; no loop can end up uncloseable by any session
tasks.notes:
Hit on 2026-08-11. Calling 'aw wrap' twice with the same --session-id writes a SECOND session file (stem gets a '-1' suffix) rather than updating the first. The second wrap then refuses '--resolves' against a loop the FIRST wrap filed, rejecting it as kind 'self' — presumably comparing session ids rather than session-file stems.

Net effect: loop '2026-08-11-1121-8f3368e6-da5a-431c-930b-00b41fefdf32#pr-stack' is open and describes work that is fully done (#103/#104 merged), and no wrap from that session can close it. Only a future session with a different id can.

Two candidate fixes, and the choice matters: (a) make a repeat wrap with the same --session-id update the existing record, which also stops the duplicate-session-record problem, or (b) narrow the self-reference check to the session FILE stem so a later wrap can close an earlier one's loops. (a) is probably the real fix; (b) alone would leave two records for one session.

tasks.title: parseTaskId invents task refs from any uppercase-hyphen-number token

Note the fix is NOT simply 'require the id to resolve against the task store' — that would make edge creation depend on the store, which AW-101 deliberately confined to a reconcile step. tasks.title: aw resume cannot find sessions that ran under a non-default profile
tasks.done_when: `aw resume <session_id>` locates and resumes a session that ran under a declared initiative profile, resolving against that profile's projects directory rather than only ~/.claude/projects.
tasks.notes:
Known gap left open by the `profile` feature shipped in 0.8.0 (PR #129).

`spawnClaudeResume` in src/aw.ts passes `process.env` unchanged, and the session lookup falls back to `~/.claude/projects`. An initiative with `profile: agents` writes its session history to `~/.claude-profiles/agents/projects`, so resume will not find it.

Two parts to fix:
1. Session lookup should search the profile's projects directory when the initiative declares one — or search all profile roots when resolving by bare session id, since the caller may not know which profile ran it.
2. `spawnClaudeResume` should apply the same `applyProfileEnv` treatment as `spawnClaude`, otherwise the resumed session runs on the wrong account even if the transcript is found.

`applyProfileEnv` in src/launcher-profile.ts is already pure and reusable for part 2.

Profile directories live under ~/.claude-profiles (CLAUDE_PROFILE_ROOT overrides the root).

tasks.title: mcp restart leaves the daemon down when its own transport drops
tasks.done_when: `active-work mcp restart` reliably leaves a daemon listening afterwards, or fails loudly enough that the caller knows to start it manually. Verified by restarting via the MCP tool and confirming port 7400 is serving without manual intervention.
tasks.notes:
Observed 2026-09-15 while upgrading to 0.8.0.

Calling `active__mcp__restart` through the MCP tool kills the daemon that is serving that very call, so the response is lost:

    MCP server "active-work" transport dropped mid-call; response for tool
    "active__mcp__restart" was lost

That much is expected. The problem is what followed: no replacement daemon came up. Port 7400 was not listening and `active-work mcp status` reported `{"running": false}`. Recovery needed a manual `active-work mcp serve --detach`.

So the restart is not just noisy on its own transport, it can leave the service down. Since the caller's response is lost either way, they have no signal that recovery is required.

Worth considering: spawn the replacement fully detached and confirm it is listening *before* stopping the old one, or have the stop path schedule the respawn so it survives the dying process. Failing that, document that a restart issued through the MCP transport must be followed by a status check.

tasks.title: Push the changesets release branch with a GitHub App token so Version Packages CI runs
tasks.done_when: titan-platform's release.yml creates the changeset-release/main PR with a GitHub App installation token, not GITHUB_TOKEN. The next Version Packages PR head reports dag-check, egress-scan, hub-compose and validate with no manual approval. The npm-publishing skill's approval step is then removed.
tasks.notes: Decided by the owner 2026-09-28: approve the waiting runs by hand for now, and set up the App later. Cause: the repo-rulesets `no-direct-push` ruleset (24143885, no bypass) requires those four checks. Changesets pushes the branch with GITHUB_TOKEN, so the runs sit in action_required. PR #173 head e0e97fd had zero check runs. The owner has to create and install the App (actions/create-github-app-token). The workflow is deliberately token-free today (release.yml line 9), so keep npm publishing on OIDC and use the App token only for the branch push. Second gate, observed by tp-messaging-design on 2026-09-29 while releasing PR #173: after the runs were approved and all four required checks were green on e0e97fd, mergeable_state stayed blocked. The ruleset has require_extra_approval_for_unattributed_changes: true and the branch commits are authored by github-actions[bot]. The state changed to clean as soon as the owner's approving review landed (02:47Z). So the App token must also produce commits GitHub counts as attributed, or every release still needs the owner's review. Verify this on the first Version Packages PR after the change. An agent cannot give that review or merge the PR in auto mode: the permission classifier denies both as self-approval.

tasks.title: Visual baselines cover 22 of 146 components; the gap silently passed a real regression
tasks.done_when: playwright.baseline.config.ts sets a stricter threshold, and a committed baseline PNG exists for MesoProgressBar, MesoCard, SegmentedBar and the ui/* primitives; changing a track alpha 0.12 to 0.50 fails the visual check.
tasks.notes:
Measured 2026-09-10. TWO compounding gaps, the second found by titan-b3 during batch B3.

(1) COVERAGE: 68 baseline PNGs cover ~22 distinct components against 146 component source files. MesoProgressBar, MesoCard, MesoStatusCard, SegmentedBar, ScheduleTiles, SessionHeader, WeekRow, WorkoutCard, VolumeLandmarkBar and every ui/* primitive have no baseline at all. PR #178 passed the visual check while changing MesoProgressBar's track alphas from 0.12 to 0.50 because it has none.

(2) SENSITIVITY, the more dangerous one: having a baseline does NOT mean being covered. packages/ui/playwright.baseline.config.ts sets maxDiffPixelRatio 0.01 and no explicit threshold, so Playwright's default per-pixel YIQ tolerance (0.2) also applies. titan-b3 initially concluded StatusDot, WeightBadge and ExerciseCard were unchanged because their baselines did not move — they had in fact changed pixels. A 0.15->0.12 rung shift and a 1px type step on an 18px dot are not counted as differing pixels at all: 18x18 is 324 px, 1% allows 3 to differ outright, and sub-threshold colour deltas are never counted.

Consequence: a green visual check is not evidence about fills or small type, whether or not a baseline exists. The B2 wash flattening passed all four gates for exactly this reason.

Decide the target: (a) tighten threshold/maxDiffPixelRatio for small components, (b) extend baselines to the components most at risk of silent colour drift, or (c) stop treating visual green as fill verification and push that assurance into token-choice assertions in vitest (the pattern that did catch things this wave). Do NOT regenerate baselines locally — container-generated from the CI artifact only.

CONCRETE MISS 2026-09-14 (AW-142 wave two PR A): collapsing Pill xs->sm would have grown nine size=xs call sites in shell/** and custom/ActiveWork/** from 4/1 to 8/2 with no failing check. Verified: visual.yml DOES gate (layer 1 test:visual:baseline fails on any pixel diff; the regen step is if: always() and only uploads a refresh artifact), but all 68 committed *-chromium-linux.png live under specimen/baseline/workout-baseline.screenshot.test.ts-snapshots, i.e. Workout only. Shell rail, NavItem, SessionStatePill and every ActiveWork component have zero baselines. Caught by a human reading the diff, not by CI.

SEQUENCING 2026-09-14 (operator): run AW-138 immediately after AW-142 wave three lands, ahead of AW-125/AW-129. Wave three is the last big pixel-moving wave; extend baselines to shell, ActiveWork and the ui primitives right after so the new spacing is locked in. Target decision (threshold vs coverage vs vitest token assertions) still open; the AW-142 waves' geometry tests are evidence for option (c) working.

SENSITIVITY DATA POINT 2026-09-14 (#232 rebase, run 34867236576): a 1px vertical padding change on InputBar (5->6) moved 2595 px = 9% of compare-input-bar-default and FAILED Layer 1 at maxDiffPixelRatio 0.01. So sensitivity is adequate for input-sized components; the gap is specific to very small components (the 18px StatusDot case) and to COVERAGE (shell/ActiveWork/ui primitives have no PNGs). Prioritise coverage over threshold tuning.

CONCRETE FILE LIST 2026-09-14 (from #234, aw142-wave3c): ZERO Layer-1 baselines exist for GoalTrajectoryChart, StrengthTrendChart, ActiveWorkoutPage, ExerciseDetailPage, ProgramPlanningPage, TrainingStatusPage. #234 moved eight legend swatch gaps 5->4 and two chart status pills 3->2 with no visual coverage at all; only the operator's Gate 2 saw it. The 68 PNGs cover Workout components plus four VelocityStrip captures. First targets for coverage: these six, plus shell/** and custom/ActiveWork/** (zero PNGs, the xs-pill near-miss), plus ui primitives.
